title: The Plan That Was Never Recalculated
teaser: The mall will hold the two spaces only until Friday. Lin Shan has four days to decide how the company should enter this northern city for the first time: sign for a two-floor flagship store, or begin with a standard store that can be renewed or exited after six months. Both options make sense on Monday. What makes the decision harder is that new information keeps arriving each day, while the signing deadline does not move.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Zhou Hang spread two floor plans and the same financial model across the meeting table. From the company’s experience in three other cities, a flagship store was more likely to build scale in the first year, and it was the only option that could reach the annual sales line headquarters had written into the plan. The standard store was expected to generate about sixty percent of the flagship’s sales, but it required far less inventory, staffing, and fixed investment, and after six months the company could renew the lease, expand, or leave. Lin Shan asked the team to recalculate both options using the same four dimensions—sales, inventory, staffing, and exit cost—and compare them again on Thursday afternoon before choosing which contract to sign.

That afternoon, Shen Ning returned with local data. Saturday traffic was nearly twice Tuesday traffic. The warehouse was more than four hundred kilometres from the store, and among comparable brands nearby, basic products sold faster than the premium range the company had planned to feature. For the first time, Zhou Hang put those numbers into both models. The flagship could still reach the sales line, but only with more basic stock and more staff assigned to weekends. The standard store’s sales ceiling had not changed, yet its smaller footprint and faster stock rotation meant lower inventory and scheduling pressure. Both plans gained new notes. Neither had been taken off the table.

On Tuesday evening, the logistics provider confirmed that emergency replenishment could take an extra day in snowy weather. On Wednesday morning, the mall sent twelve months of hourly footfall data, showing an even wider gap between weekdays and weekends than the first estimate had suggested. At the same time, headquarters asked the team to include in Thursday’s signing package an operating plan capable of supporting the annual sales target. With only a day and a half left before the mall released the spaces, the team treated the flagship as the working option and began testing, item by item, whether it could still reach the number: hold one extra week of basic stock, add temporary weekend staff, concentrate promotions on Saturdays, and place replenishment orders one day earlier. The standard store was not rejected. It was left beside them for the final comparison.

By Thursday noon, every new risk had an answer. Slower logistics meant more inventory. Weekend congestion meant more staffing. A slower premium range meant less display space. Zhou Hang fed the measures and their costs back into the flagship forecast one by one, and the sales line was still within reach. With only a few hours before signing, everyone’s remaining time went into completing that operating package. The standard-store plan was still sitting on the figures from its first Monday update. At three in the afternoon, Lin Shan signed the flagship contract. When administration cleared the table, the standard-store plan and its old calculation sheet went together into a transparent folder.

When the store opened in November, almost everything that happened had already appeared on those Wednesday notes. Saturday traffic was strong. Basic products came close to selling out twice, and the extra week of stock absorbed the pressure. One snow day delayed transport by a day, but earlier replenishment kept the shelves from going empty. The premium range sold slowly, so the team reduced its display space and moved two promotional events to Saturday. The responses did not fail, and there was no obvious execution mistake on the floor. By month-end, total sales were only slightly below plan. The extra inventory, temporary staffing, and transport expense needed to protect those sales also appeared, one line at a time, almost exactly as forecast.

At the quarterly review, the sales page came first: 24 percent of the annual target had been achieved, close to the planned pace. The next pages accumulated inventory carrying cost, additional shifts, campaign spending, and expedited transport. The profit target stood at only 15 percent. Most of the gap came from the same measures added three months earlier to keep the flagship capable of reaching the sales line. Lin Shan set the report aside and pulled the transparent folder from the file rack. She laid the standard-store plan, untouched for three months, beside the flagship plan again. In its lower-right corner were still the two words written on Monday: “six months.”
concept: COSO Enterprise Risk Management (COSO ERM 2017) emphasizes that risk information should enter strategic choice, objective setting, and performance judgment, rather than only the execution controls applied after a strategy has already been chosen. An organization may design effective responses to risk, but if new information is used only to prove that the original option can still reach a target, without changing the comparison among strategic alternatives, risk management and strategy can gradually separate.
explanation: The key issue in the story is not that the flagship store was executed badly, but that the comparison process changed direction. On Monday, both market-entry options were compared across the same dimensions. From Wednesday onward, the signing deadline and the headquarters sales target pushed the team to concentrate its limited time on one question: how can the flagship still reach the sales line? New risks were therefore converted into measures for inventory, staffing, promotion, and transport. Those measures worked, but they also changed the cost and profit assumptions, while the standard-store option was no longer recalculated with the same new information. The quarterly result reveals not a failed response, but a strategic comparison frozen at an older version.
mapping: Two floor plans and one shared calculation sheet → In the normal state, both strategic options are compared at the same time across sales, resource commitment, and exit conditions.

Headquarters requires an operating plan that supports the annual sales target, while the Friday signing deadline approaches → The team reasonably directs its limited time toward proving the flagship remains feasible, shifting behaviour from “compare the options” to “complete one option.”

Inventory, staffing, promotions, and earlier replenishment all work as planned → This rules out simple execution failure. The responses protect sales, but they also raise the resources and costs required to achieve those sales.

Sales progress at 24%, profit progress at 15%, while the standard-store model is still at its Monday version → The visible target is nearly on track, but new risk information has not continued to enter a like-for-like comparison of the strategic alternatives.
boundary: The story does not prove that the standard store would have been better than the flagship, nor does it suggest that organizations should reduce scale whenever risk appears. The flagship might still be more reasonable because of growth objectives, brand exposure, or long-term value. The issue being tested is the decision process: when risk responses materially change resource needs, costs, and performance assumptions, does the organization still compare strategic options using the updated information, or does it ask only how the chosen plan can keep meeting its target?
reflection: If the same assumptions about traffic, inventory, staffing, and transport had been put back into the standard-store model on Thursday noon, would the two plans still have been as far apart as they were on Monday?
